extracted.intended_audience: general readers, law students, and legal researchers interested in U.S. labor law and Supreme Court cases
extracted.subtask_description: A concise encyclopedia-style summary of a U.S. Supreme Court decision (facts, legal issue, statutory/regulatory provisions at issue, holding, and case history) focused on Fair Labor Standards Act and related Department of Labor regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 29 U.S.C. §213(a)(15) — companionship services exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fair Labor Standards Act exemption under 29 U.S.C. §213(a)(15) exempts persons 'employed in domestic service employment to provide companionship services for individuals ... unable to care for themselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory exemption is the central statutory text at issue: employers argued they were not required to pay minimum wage because employees fell within this exemption. Evaluate whether the worker's duties and employment context fall within the statutory language as interpreted by courts and agency regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department of Labor General Regulations §552.3 — 'private home' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Department of Labor General Regulations §552.3 states the companionship exemption applies only when services are performed in the 'private home ... of the person by whom he or she is employed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The DOL regulation narrows the statutory exemption by requiring the services be performed in the employer's private home. In this case the regulation's meaning and applicability were dispositive; the Supreme Court held the regulation was 'valid and binding.' When analyzing similar disputes, determine whether services occurred in the private home as defined by the regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron deference to agency interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should defer to a reasonable agency interpretation of an ambiguous statute (Chevron deference). The Supreme Court held the Department of Labor's regulation was entitled to deference and was 'valid and binding,' and that the Second Circuit should have applied Chevron.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a statute is ambiguous, evaluate whether the agency interpretation is reasonable and thus entitled to Chevron deference. The case demonstrates that an agency regulation clarifying statutory scope (here, the companionship exemption) can be dispositive and binding on courts unless unreasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of FLSA minimum wage requirements to domestic/companionship workers
rubrics_metrics.description: The overarching legal question is whether domestic workers providing companionship services are entitled to the FLSA minimum wage or fall within the statutory/regulatory exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze factual circumstances (location of work, nature of services, employer-employee relationship) against the statutory exemption and DOL regulations; this case resolved that the DOL regulation limiting the exemption was valid, affecting whether employers must pay minimum wage for such workers.
